results.pageDescription: President Donald Trump’s campaign promises for mass deportation and building a border wall are in the works, but he has broken other pledges.
results.evidenceText: After midterm elections, Trump said he was ‘too tough’ on immigration. Here’s what he’s done so far – PolitiFact Skip to content Stand up for the facts! Our only agenda is to publish the truth so you can be an informed participant in democracy. We need your help. More Info I would like to contribute $ One Time Monthly Yearly Join Now! After midterm elections, Trump said he was ‘too tough’ on immigration. Here’s what he’s done so far 2026 Midterms Border Security Immigration National Read in English A group of immigrants stand by as they are processed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents before deportation across the McAllen–Hidalgo–Reynosa International Bridge in McAllen, Texas, March 13, 2026. (AP) By Maria Briceño November 10, 2026 By Amy Sherman November 10, 2026 In his first sit-down interview after the midterm elections where his party resoundingly lost control of both chambers of Congress, President Donald Trump both acknowledged that his immigration agenda might have turned away some voters and praised it. CBS News’ “60 Minutes” correspondent Ross Douthat asked Trump if his immigration crackdown hurt Republicans in the elections. “I think it both helped and hurt,” Trump said in the interview that aired Nov. 8. “I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out.” But the administration also removed “people that had good jobs” in landscaping or hotels, in some cases people who paid taxes, he said, and that hurt the party. Trump, who said he had been “too tough” on immigration, said he would work out an immigration “deal” with Democrats, but provided no details. After the Nov. 3 election, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin floated the idea of working with Congress on a legal pathway for immigrants who came to the U.S. illegally as children and who are protected from deportation under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, or DACA. On Nov. 9, Trump told reporters “we’re not going to have amnesty or anything” for immigrants illegally in the country. Trump has promoted Stephen Miller, his former deputy chief of staff, as his new chief of staff. Miller led Trump’s first-term hard-line immigration agenda, supporting policies that separated families arriving at the border and that banned the entry of people from several Muslim-majority countries. During Trump’s second term, Miller has been a leading architect of Trump’s immigration strategy and has pushed the administration to arrest at least 3,000 immigrants a day. Immigration experts doubt that Trump will cool down on enforcement as Miller embraces his new role. “Promoting Stephen Miller hardly signals a retreat from the administration’s mass deportation agenda,” said Tom K. Wong, director of the U.S. Immigration Policy Center at the University of California, San Diego. “ Until we see actual changes in enforcement priorities, the president’s remarks seem more like a change in political messaging than a change in policy.” PolitiFact has tracked Trump’s progress on immigration campaign promises on our MAGA-Meter . Here’s a look at where Trump’s immigration promises stand. Haitians deported from the United States deplane at the international airport in Cap-Haitien, Haiti, Aug. 27, 2026. (AP) Promise: Carry out the largest domestic deportation operation in American history This is In the Works. The Department of Homeland Security said that as of October, the administration had deported about 1.2 million immigrants during Trump’s second term. Immigration experts say it’s hard to independently verify the scale of deportations, because the administration isn’t releasing monthly or comprehensive data. The Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank, analyzed DHS data and estimated that from January 2025 to July 31, the administration deported about 980,000 people. The institute said that on an annual basis, while the total deportations are up from the Biden and first Trump administrations, they remain below the levels from the early 2000s. The Deportation Data Project at the University of California, Los Angeles, and the University of California, Berkeley, obtained data from ICE showing the agency arrested and detained about 42,000 people in July, a monthly record during this term. A substantial proportion of those arrested within the country are people who lived in the U.S. for more than a decade, said Elizabeth Cohen, a Boston University political science professor. “ Trump‘s immigration agenda has dramatically expanded an already costly interior enforcement apparatus,” Cohen said, although most deportations continue to originate at the border, and border encounters have fallen sharply from Biden administration levels. A U.S. Border Patrol truck drives past a section of border wall, Sept. 17, 2026, in Mission, Texas. (AP) Promise: Finish the border wall This is In the Works. DHS reported Nov. 3 that from the beginning of Trump’s second term in late January 2025 through Oct. 30, U.S. Customs and Border Protection completed approximately 330 miles of new border barriers. This includes 139.5 miles of primary wall that faces Mexico, 73.9 miles of waterborne barrier , which are usually floating infrastructure placed in bodies of water along the southern border; and 116.2 miles of secondary wall, barriers behind the already existing primary walls to add an additional obstacle. On Nov. 9, the Supreme Court ruled the Trump administration can continue with border wall construction along the southern border in the Big Bend region of Southwest Texas, which environmentalists say could harm wildlife and the area’s residents. It lifted a district judge’s order from October that halted construction. Since Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on July 4, 2025, which included funding to build the border wall, CBP has awarded 11 contracts to build segments of new wall and detection technology. CBP says the money awarded in part is for building a “smart wall,” which is a mixture of steel walls, roads, detection technology, cameras and lighting. CBP has designated $34.6 billion of the law’s funding for the border wall. Promise: Revoke the temporary legal status of Haitians This is In the Works. In a 6-3 vote in June, the Supreme Court paved the way for the administration to revoke Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status designation, which protected hundreds of thousands of Haitians from deportation. In recent months, about 1,000 of the 350,000 people with TPS have been deported to Haiti, according to Human Rights Watch, which cited Haiti’s National Migration Office. Haitians were also deported to Mexico in 2025 and 2026. Trump made this promise in 2024 as he and his running mate JD Vance spread the lie that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were stealing and eating people’s pets. A local student named Shama holds a sign during a vigil to mark the anniversary of Haiti’s 2010 earthquake, and support of Temporary Protected Status for Haitians, Jan. 12, 2026, in the Little Haiti neighborhood of Miami. (AP) Promise: Restore and expand the travel ban This is a Promise Kept. During his first term, Trump used executive orders to impose travel bans on people from seven countries, suspending their visas for 90 days. After a legal battle, the Supreme Court ruled that the president can issue a travel ban under certain circumstances. President Joe Biden revoked the ban; Trump resurrected it in his second term and expanded it to 19 countries. Promise: Restore Remain in Mexico program This is a Promise Broken. Biden in 2021 terminated Trump’s first-term Migrant Protection Protocol, aka Remain in Mexico program. In January 2025, at the start of his second term, Trump signed an executive order to reinstate the program , which sent certain migrants seeking asylum to Mexico to await their U.S. immigration court proceedings. On Oct. 7, a federal court ruled the program’s implementation is unlawful. The Trump administration has not appealed this decision. Promise: Require proof of citizenship at the polls This is a Promise Broken. Trump lobbied for the passage of the SAVE America Act . The legislation would require people to provide documentary proof of citizenship, such as a passport or birth certificate, when registering to vote. It passed the House in February but stalled in the Senate. It’s unlikely that the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress will pass this legislation. results.pageDescription: 'You Can See Everything' actor Amanda Seyfried joins co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim to discuss making the hit Elizabeth Holmes doc.
results.evidenceText: Amanda Seyfried and Nathan Fielder on 'You Can See Everything' × × Skip to main content Add us as a Google Preferred Source Editor’s note: This article contains major spoilers for the documentary “You Can See Everything.” “Well, guys, what should we talk about?” This is a joke offered by one of three people on a Zoom with Rolling Stone one October afternoon. Because like virtually everybody who’s been to the movies in the past month, and even many who haven’t, the subject these three are most keen to chat about is the brain-boggling, meme-launching, WTF-did-I-just-watch documentary You Can See Everything .  If you haven’t seen it yet, you undoubtedly know the elevator pitch: Nathan Fielder embeds himself in the home of convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, right before Holmes reports to prison. You also know the major conversation-starter moments: The shower scene. The egg-whipping. The abundant close-ups of unblinking stares. The one thing that makes this virtual coffee klatch a little different is that the folks ready to discuss the ins and outs of this cultural phenomenon include Fielder and his co-director, Lance Oppenheim . And if you’re among the many, many folks who’ve helped turn this gonzo experiment in nonfiction filmmaking into a blockbuster, you can likely guess who the third person in the chat might be. Hint: It’s not Holmes. Rather, it’s the woman who’s played her not once, but now twice — Amanda Seyfried , the Dropout star whose presence in the documentary’s second half has been one of the best-kept moviegoing secrets in recent memory, and the aspect that sends it into a whole new stratosphere of mind-fuckery.  Seyfried joined her co-conspirators for an exclusive conversation — her first time on the record about the film, and the first time the three collaborators have discussed it since the premiere — to talk about how she was drawn into the project, that awkward on-camera phone call with Holmes, and how they’ve all been processing the experience. Making and releasing the film has been an emotional roller coaster for each of them (Oppenheim says it “made my brain and body feel on fire”), but Seyfried, for one, has enjoyed the ride. “I have no regrets,” she says. “I’m having the time of my life right now!” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. Oppenheim: Well, where should we start?  Seyfried: My first question is: What am I doing here? What am I doing in this movie? How did I get here? Fielder: That’s a great question, Amanda. How did you get here? SACHA LECCA Oppenheim: I feel like there was a certain point in the process of making this where we wanted to expand the bubble [of people involved in the project]. But so many of the people we reached out to didn’t want to be on camera because Elizabeth had this toxic reputation. Fielder: This was two years after we had shot in that beach house with them. We were just like, “Where do we go next?” The Dropout kept coming up. Elizabeth’s parents really had very strong feelings about it, and they felt it was one of the main ways the general public knew about who Elizabeth Holmes was. So we thought it would be interesting to talk to you. I got your phone number through Emma Stone. We had a 30-minute Zoom, and you were like, “Yeah, come over with cameras.” We wanted to show you what became the first half of the film, and then we would talk about it. That’s all you agreed to. Related Content Despite Fallout, Billy Evans Would ‘100%’ Do ‘You Can See Everything’ Again Billy Evans Reveals He's a Fan of 'You Can See Everything' Despite Villainous Portrayal ‘SNL’: Druski Impersonates ‘Crazy’ Elizabeth Holmes in Meta-Documentary Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner Did an AMA About That Shower Scene, His Sniffing, and ‘You Can See Everything’ The crazy thing to me [was that] you didn’t go through any talent reps or anyone. You just said, “Yeah, come over!” Why did you trust us like that? Seyfried: I remember when [Emma] texted, and I was like, “Nathan Fielder? Ooh, I wonder if he wants to make something with me?” My sister is a big fan [of yours, Nathan], and I know a lot of people are big fans of Nathan for You . I’d only seen The Curse. When you said you had 90 minutes of footage for me to see and help you work through, I was like, “Oh, he just wants some advice. He just wants us to know about my experience playing her and researching her and going into the mind of that quote-unquote character I portrayed.” After the Zoom, I was totally game to do whatever you needed. It was just your energy [that persuaded me], and how much time you had spent [on this project], and that nobody knew this was happening. “It felt dangerous. I wanted answers. We all had this need to understand who was pulling the strings.” Amanda Seyfried Oppenheim: Weren’t you nervous? Seyfried: I wasn’t nervous. There were just way more people than I expected coming into my apartment [ laughs ]. I had just gotten back from the Venice Film Festival, and I said this is the only time I can do it; I’m just never in the city. I didn’t know how long it was going to take. I thought, “Wait a minute, there’s cameras. I should probably put on some mascara …” There was no protection. There was no advocate for me. I just felt like I was totally game because I was so invested in what you were doing, and already had this strange level of trust in you guys. Fielder: It’s not dissimilar to Elizabeth, I guess, who also just had a strange level of trust. SACHA LECCA Seyfried: Not dissimilar … but not super similar, I would say. Fielder: Thanks for clarifying [ laughs ]. Seyfried: I would say there was a lot of risk in the back of my head, and then when I told my agent and lawyer that I had already done it? Not the normal process [ laughs ]. But I go off and do my own thing sometimes, and nobody had any say or control over what I was doing with Nathan and Lance. My lawyer was like, “Well, now we have to retroactively set your deal in place because you need protection.” We weren’t even considering reenactments at that point. Fielder: We should clarify that because, yeah, all you’d agreed to was just coming in, and we’d show you the stuff and talk. Seyfried: I wasn’t even a subject at that point. Oppenheim: I think you said that you’d never play this person again. When we started showing you that stuff — there was a moment in the conversation where you started imitating her on camera, and you gave Nathan this look. What brought you back into that? Seyfried: Muscle memory. I think the reason I was able to capture my version of Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout was not her Nightline interview, or 60 Minutes, or whatever footage I’d seen. It was the 10 hours of deposition tapes, where she was present and completely consistent. That’s the thing that my brain is locked into. So even though it had been a bunch of years, I see her again in the footage … and I can’t help but tilt my head a little bit. It’s muscle memory when you play a character as intensely as I did for as long as I did. I do think there’s something almost uncontrollable. When I was talking to you, it was already coming out of me in some way. “It wasn’t until I was sitting across from you in those re-creations that I realized how well I understood Liz’s tendencies.” Nathan Fielder Fielder: You said you wouldn’t play her again, and then you started doing it — but you never actually said you would play her again. It’s so interesting, because the process of making this was to try to give as much information as we could to the audience on how we interpreted these moments that were happening in the house and with her. Anything that didn’t happen on camera, we took notes of. But we were talking about the oddness of these early meetings, and we always assumed that, well, obviously these things can’t be part of the film. But then we were sort of like, “Wait, would the idea of doing a re-creation work?” At first we didn’t even consider it because we thought it was a little lame, maybe, to do these types of things. But the way you engaged with it when we shot at your apartment, it felt to us like there was something in you. It was like you wanted to revisit it. Oppenheim: It felt like you had unfinished business — like it was pouring out of you. You were unresolved or something. Fielder: Did you have something unresolved? Seyfried: Don’t we all? [ Laughs. ] I mean, now that people have seen the movie, isn’t everybody kind of feeling that? That’s the thing about how powerful this whole project is, the nuance of it and its capacity to be all things. You can’t resolve any of it. You can learn about how you feel and you can learn about your perspective on things, but … It’s not that I was unresolved; it’s that I had more information now because of [your] footage. Anybody who’s watched this documentary knows that the first 90 [minutes] or so, there’s a lot of information there. So the idea that I could go on this journey with you guys, however you needed me, in whatever capacity, was very interesting to me. SACHA LECCA Fielder: We started having conversations about: “OK, would you portray her again?” All I said was that we’d want you to re-create some initial conversations that happened off-camera. But then we also said, because this is a documentary, we didn’t want to discuss these scenes or show you scripts in advance. We just want you to show up, and we’ll talk about the scenes on camera. Anything that comes up in those conversations will potentially be part of it. People should know that you had no creative control over this project. Anything that was filmed— Seyfried: No approval. Whatsoever. Fielder: You had no approval over anything. You were just engaging with these scenes for the first time. Were you nervous at any point during this? Seyfried: Yes! I mean, there was always this vibration of risk and that sensation of: Am I going to destroy my career in some way? Am I going to get entangled in this, like, wasp’s nest with Billy? Am I gonna say the wrong thing? Am I gonna perpetuate negativity for her? Everything was scary, but I still had that drive that was more in the front seat — which was the literal front seat with you in the car. I was just like, “Let’s go, buddy! I want to put my hand in the fire!” Fielder: We just had planned to do those first few re-creations, the meeting and the one at the house. Nothing beyond that. And then you were getting drawn in, and it seemed like you had to go to Billy. You’re now in this process, and it’s not like we can drive this thing forward because so much is based on your comfort level. What made you want to keep going beyond those re-creations? Seyfried: I don’t know. I don’t know. It’s the same as whatever was driving you guys this whole time. Fielder: Why did you want to meet Billy? Seyfried: I just … [ pauses ]. It felt dangerous. I wanted answers. We all had this need to understand who was pulling the strings. What he was doing and how he was in the footage that I saw, how you guys were interacting — it felt yucky to me. I just wanted any information I could get on Billy. I became this weird Billy detective because I had gotten such strong negative feelings from him in the footage. I felt like I needed to meet this guy. It was exciting to me, and it was scary, and it was questionable. You wanted that, too, but it had to come from me because I don’t think you would have put me in that position. I did feel protected by you guys pretty early on. I felt like I trusted you. Even though I kept jokingly saying, “You’re not going to ruin my life, right?” SACHA LECCA Fielder: And what was my answer? I forget. Seyfried: “I’m not trying to. But maybe.” [ Laughs. ] Just kidding. Fielder: That sounds like what I would say, actually. Oppenheim: It was such a gigantic leap of faith. I don’t know if you know how amazing and also how insane it was that you were willing to put yourself out there in this way. Seyfried: But I want people to know that it wasn’t like I jumped into the deep end. It was a process. “What are you doing on this date?” “I don’t know. I’m busy on this date, but I’m around on this date?” “OK, let’s meet here.” So it was just a step-by-step process. It wasn’t like a script, and we were going to shoot it. I wasn’t committing to shooting a movie. I was committing to each event or moment, and those are little leaps of faith that ended up feeling bigger. Oppenheim: If you’re saying you’re a “Billy detective,” what did you feel after you met him? Did your feelings change at all? Seyfried: Nothing changed. It only got worse. That’s very clear in the doc, I think. Fielder: Did you feel like, “Oh, he’s different?” Or were you like, “He’s the same guy I saw in that footage?” Seyfried: I had to put on a different hat [when I met him]. I was filtered. I wouldn’t necessarily call it acting, but … I was thinking about how I wanted to protect myself, but I also wanted to give the guy a chance to be as he is. I wanted to turn my disdain off a little bit, because I’m in his house now with his children — with their children. I always want to give people the benefit of the doubt, and I felt bad that I had talked a bunch of shit about him up until that point.  Because look, I do not like him. But I’m coming into this man’s house. I just wanted to be a presence, the way that you guys are so good at being present in these situations. But you also knew him. The whole crew knew him, and he knew them. Billy doesn’t know me at all. He just assumes many things about me, which is normal. So I’m just trying to engage with him, and it’s fine. It’s going fine. And then [Elizabeth] calls, and that was just … what an experience for somebody to have, to say the least. Everything I’m feeling, you can see. I don’t even have to describe it to you. “The moment that I’ll probably be thinking about on my deathbed is the dinner scene between you and Billy.” Lance Oppenheim Fielder: I want people to know that everything that’s outside of the scripted reenactments, that’s all coming from you — we’re not saying, “Well, you have to say this or that” in any of these things. This is all just happening in real time. Seyfried: We didn’t know she was gonna call right then. And I am sitting there with her children and cuddling with her dog! While she’s in prison! And then she calls, and … Someone asked me if that was real, if that was really her on the phone. And I’m like, “It’s a documentary. Who else would it be?” Oppenheim: Every time I watch the movie, it feels like your performance in the reenactments evolves, from that first one to the final one. Seyfried: From insecurity to … um, security. [ Laughs. ] SACHA LECCA Oppenheim: Did anything change over the course of it? Was it something in the way you prepared, or did experiencing all the stuff you did with us impact anything? Seyfried: I think it had to do with intensity. I mean, that last scene in the prison is all from Nathan’s memory. [ To Nathan ] You did an amazing job trying to remember everything. Fielder: The second I got out [of the visiting room], I recorded everything I could remember into my phone. Seyfried: You did your due diligence with that. I think the stakes were so high at that point for all of us because it had just happened. The reenactments I was doing from the beginning … [they] were things that had happened when you were with them years prior. I was still insecure about it, and I was like, “I don’t know if I can still do the voice.” Also, the audience will have just seen her for 90 minutes — how are they gonna just suspend disbelief? It was very much like, “How am I going to do this? I don’t know if I can capture her anymore.” And then by the end, I had been doing it enough, and I really had a good time in the pizza house doing the A24 meeting [scene]. I really got my stride, and then the stakes were so high because you had literally just gone to the prison. For most of the filming, we were like, “When are you gonna go? When can you go?” Fielder: We were really focused on trying to get cameras in there because it was really frustrating to have these things that kept happening off-camera that were so relevant to our understanding. We were hopeful for a time that we could get cameras in there, but … I mean, you see it a little bit in the movie where I wasn’t excited about doing a re-creation of that final visit. Also, there was a rumor online that I had visited her before. That is bad information. I had never visited her in prison before that one [visit portrayed] in the film. So, just to clarify that. Anyway, I was nervous about re-creating that because the earlier re-creations were more about describing what happened in the house and in those early meetings. This one was: I’m asking her questions, and the way she responds and the expression on her face is what would be telling [the audience] about it. I was really skeptical that those things could be captured in a re-creation without it feeling goofy, or just, like, so detached from reality. It was the best we could do given all the constraints on access to her. But then — and I don’t know if I ever told you this, Amanda — but it wasn’t until I was sitting across from you in those re-creations that I realized how well I understood Liz’s tendencies. Because when anything was slightly off in what you were doing, we would talk about it. It was really like, “This is not how it was.” Seyfried: You were so specific. SACHA LECCA Fielder: But when you got it, it was like, “Wow. This is it. This is what I experienced.” I never thought that would be possible in a re-creation. Really, it’s a testament to your performance. You came in with choices that you were making as a performer, which is great. But sometimes it would be off from what I had witnessed, and so we’d adjust until we got it right, and then it was incredible when you hit it. Even the way you responded to the questions when it was, like, almost nonanswers and certain things, it’s exactly how she answered. Seyfried: Do you remember when we were in the barn and you were telling me I was doing it wrong? I remember that at one point I’m like, “ How was it done, Nathan?? ”  Oppenheim: There’s an amazing expression on your face where it’s like, “Come on, man, which way is it ?”  The performance you’re doing here — even though you’ve done the character before, it feels different than anything else you’ve ever done. I remember being behind the monitor for the final reenactment, and I did feel like I was seeing her. It was startling. Seyfried: How did you edit together, like, 700 hours of footage? There could have been 1,000 versions of this movie. “I am sitting there with her children and cuddling with her dog! While she’s in prison! And then she calls!” Amanda Seyfried Oppenheim: This happened when we were shooting, but especially when we were in the edit room with Adam Locke-Norton — who’s edited a lot of Nathan’s stuff — we would gravitate toward the moments that we most disagreed on.  Fielder: “Disagreed on” in terms of what we were witnessing. results.evidenceText: More Than 1,300 Diplomatic Passports Missing in Vanuatu, Report Finds | OCCRP Power and Influence • Vanuatu More Than 1,300 Diplomatic Passports Missing in Vanuatu, Report Finds A parliamentary inquiry implicated top government officials in the improper issuance of the documents to foreign nationals. Banner: Phillip Capper/Flickr | View of Port Vila,Vanuatu’s capital. Reported by Hilaire Bule OCCRP November 12, 2026 | 3 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious A damning parliamentary report in Vanuatu has found more than 1,300 diplomatic passports went missing in recent years and remain unaccounted for. The report by Vanuatu’s Public Accounts Committee, released on Tuesday and obtained by OCCRP, revealed that 1,390 diplomatic passports went missing between 2019 and 2024, with 1,301 disappearing in 2024 alone. The committee also found significant irregularities in the processing and issuance of the documents, including alleged misuse by the country’s prime minister and foreign minister. It is the latest passport controversy for the small Pacific island country of roughly 340,000 people, whose so-called “golden passport” program has attracted a colorful cast of wealthy investors ranging from spies and fugitives to sanctioned oligarchs and influencer Andrew Tate . The report followed several years of mounting concerns over the country’s issuance of diplomatic passports. The committee found that Prime Minister Jotham Napat, Foreign Minister Marc Ati, and other top officials improperly appointed foreign nationals as special envoys and trade commissioners. The officials granted them diplomatic status and passports without fulfilling proper residency requirements or legal mandates. The allegations against Napat date to his tenure as foreign minister. Napat and Ati did not respond to the committee’s requests for comment. When contacted by OCCRP, Ati declined to comment and Napat’s office did not respond. The report also found that amendments to Vanuatu’s Passport Act improperly bypassed the Council of Ministers, or cabinet, and contravened international conventions on diplomatic missions and officers. The amendments also violated Vanuatu’s constitutional provisions regarding public office holders and dual citizens, the report found. The irregularities were underscored by a visit committee members took to the passport office, where they “observed that the building and room hosting the passports stock and the passport office is not at all appropriate in all respects for a passport office nor was it adequately secured and safe.” “There is no camera installed internally and on the exterior of the building to ensure appropriate security maintenance,” the report continued. The report cited specific cases, including the January 2023 appointment of Chinese national Han Hans as Vanuatu’s special envoy on trade and investment to Australia, New Zealand and Singapore by then-Foreign Minister Napat. At the time, special envoys were not eligible for diplomatic passports. Nonetheless, a week later Hans collected his passport directly from Napat rather than the chief protocol officer legally authorized to distribute them, according to the report. Hans was arrested in China on August 22, 2023 after traveling on his Vanuatu diplomatic passport and later prosecuted and sentenced, according to the report, which did not specify the charges. The committee provided recommendations to hold officials accountable, cancel unlawful citizenships and passports—which Vanuatu began doing last year—and strictly overhaul internal security controls to safeguard national sovereignty. This is not the first passport embarrassment for Vanuatu. In addition to being on the European Union’s taxhaven blacklist, Vanuatu lost visa-free access to the EU in December 2024 over serious security and migration risks, inadequate applicant screening, fast processing times and instances where citizenship was granted to individuals listed in Interpol databases. Last year, OCCRP revealed that Andrew Tate, an influencer and self-described “misogynist,” had obtained a Vanuatu passport via its citizenship-by-investment scheme, which costs as little as $130,000 and comes with few restrictions. He received the document around the time of his 2022 arrest by Romanian authorities on charges including rape and human trafficking. results.pageDescription: A photograph that captures the reality of our political moment. Plus, an AI-generated reflection of Islamophobia from The Free Press, and a dystopian documentary on male body image.
results.evidenceText: Picture Perfect - Columbia Journalism Review b Ray Russell campaigner Noah Derucher and onlookers view election results at a Democratic watch party. (Photo: Noah Williford) Laurels and Darts b Sign up for the daily CJR newsletter . Sometimes an image captures a moment, and a mood, perfectly. That was the case last week when Noah Williford , a photographer for The Appalachian , Appalachian State University’s independent student paper, took the picture above at FizzEd, a bar in Boone, North Carolina, on the night of the midterm elections. “You could feel this vibe shift,” Williford told me. “It felt like this representation of what was going on nationally in this little bar and restaurant downtown.” Williford told me that The Appalachian , founded in 1934, fills an important local news gap. “A lot of smaller newspapers are owned by larger companies and are letting go of staff or increasing prices. People in places like Appalachia are going to look for news that they both can trust and can afford. And that historically is student media,” he said. “Not just across Appalachia, but also across the state of North Carolina, people are increasingly looking to their local college newspaper, their local college radio station.” Williford’s picture gained national attention when Chris Moody, one of his professors at Appalachian State, posted it on X with the caption: “This photo from Election Night in Boone, North Carolina, is a modern Norman Rockwell painting.” The post now has more than twenty-four thousand likes. Williford said he grabbed the shot just as people in the room learned that the New York Times had flipped its prediction in North Carolina’s Fifth Congressional District race, from Virginia Foxx, a Republican who has held office since 2005, to her Democratic challenger, Chuck Hubbard. (As of press time for this column, the race had yet to be called.) “The thing that makes me grin about it, especially in today’s day and age, is that it’s shockingly earnest. It’s people who decided to go out on a Tuesday night just with the hope of something good, you know? There’s no cynicism,” Williford told me. “You realize this blue wave, as we call it, is thousands of people across the United States, collectively trying to believe in something different.” It was not just the White House and MAGA Republicans who had a no-good, very-bad week last week. The Free Press , Bari Weiss’s erstwhile blog, which Paramount acquired for roughly a hundred and fifty million dollars last year, had a run of editorial mistakes that suggested a stunning lack of basic journalistic standards. On Tuesday night, Olivia Reingold, a Free Press writer who was once described as “Bari Weiss’s most loyal soldier,” broke the “news” on X that she had spotted “Valentino heels, a Chanel bag, a Moncler jacket, Rolex watches, and a YSL bag among other designer items” at what she said was “Abdul El-Sayed’s election night event.” The post included a picture of a woman’s feet in Valentino Rockstud leather heels and a quilted gold Chanel bag. The implication, I think, was that Reingold was exposing hypocrisy among the champagne crowd at El-Sayed’s party. Whatever the aim, within an hour she posted a curious clarification: the woman photographed was not at Senator-elect El-Sayed’s election party, she was at a “party for the entire Michigan Democratic Party, so it’s a data point for the entire state apparatus, not just Abdul El-Sayed’s camp.” What was the data point exactly? Who knows. But given the Islamaphobic bent of Reingold’s previous coverage, the signs point to something racist.  That was not the end of it. Social media sleuths quickly pointed out that the photo was AI-generated. ( Vanity Fair published an impressive forensic fashion analysis on why the items were not authentic.) Two days later, Reingold posted what I suppose qualifies as a second clarification: “Hello my name is Olivia Reingold and I used ChatGPT to brighten and sharpen an image of a woman in Valentino shoes and a Chanel bag. After processing, it still shows these same things: a woman wearing Valentino shoes and a Chanel bag. She is a real (and chic!) woman, really wearing those items. The observation holds.” She still has not told us what, exactly, the observation was supposed to be. The AI image is still on her feed.  If Reingold understands that using AI to “brighten and sharpen an image” is generally not acceptable practice in news, you certainly wouldn’t know it from her note, which gives the impression that she is more affronted by being held to a journalistic standard than concerned about having violated one. A spokesperson for The Free Press did not respond to a question about whether the publication, as an entity of CBS News, has any policy governing the use of AI, particularly when it comes to producing or altering photographs. Reingold, who was last seen filming herself (rather than the scene) at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner shooting, rose to Free Press fame with popular influencer-style videos. Lately, Maya Sulkin, another Free Press reporter, has joined her ranks. Last Wednesday, Sulkin posted a reaction video to The Free Press ’s X account in which she blankly watched El-Sayed’s victory speech and declared that he had delivered it in Arabic. She also implied that Ilhan Omar, the representative from Minnesota, delivered her speech in Somali, and concluded that Americans had just elected “socialist and Islamist people who don’t share American values and want to completely change America.” After viewers of the video complained, a community note was added to the post: “Apart from his own name spoken idiomatically with Arabic pronunciation, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed used four Arabic words in his victory speech, which represents 0.27% of the words he spoke.”  The Free Press first added a correction on X, saying the video was inaccurate (but not adding anything where the video appeared on Facebook, Instagram, or TikTok), before finally deleting the post two days later. In a statement, The Free Press said it had taken down the video because it “contained a factual error and its tone fell short of what we believe advances healthy public discourse” and did not meet the standards of the outlet’s “rigorous editorial process.” A spokesperson declined to answer questions about the editorial and ethical standards at The Free Press and CBS News, describe the editorial process referenced, or clarify whether anyone at the publication would face consequences for the incident, including Sulkin. You might reasonably think that that was finally the end of it. You’d be wrong. Anand Giridharadas revealed on social media late last week that he had recorded a podcast interview with Reingold about his new book, Man in the Mirror, that hadn’t been released, and suggested it had been shelved for ideological reasons. “It was about the Jordan Neely/Daniel Penny case, which we both covered,” Giridharadas posted. “It was a powerful conversation because there were real differences.” When I reached out to him, Giridharadas told me that he had done the interview precisely because he hoped “to try to get out of echo chambers.” ( The Free Press did not respond to my questions about this, either.) The Free Press is no longer the small, contrarian digital darling that helped Weiss improbably ascend to the top spot at CBS News. For better or worse, it is now part of a global news operation that is supposed to display the highest editorial integrity. One way Weiss could demonstrate that she is up to the task would be to demand that the publications and journalists she oversees adhere to exacting standards. But, to do that, she’d have to see the value in it. As Giridharadas told me, “I would just say to Bari and the leadership, they right now have a scandal of publishing fake AI-generated content. They should feel proud that the content they generated with me was the opposite of AI. It was two human beings, deeply grappling across difference and having the conversation. And if they are more comfortable publishing fake photographs than real conversations, she has ceased to be the person she promised she would be.” If you’re even moderately aware of online culture, you’ve probably heard of Clavicular, the influencer widely regarded as the world’s number one “looksmaxxer.” For the uninitiated, looksmaxxing is a subculture, popular among young men and adolescent boys, built on obsessive pursuit of physical perfection, a phenomenon that evolved out of incel communities and the manosphere. As The Atlantic ’s Ali Breland told CJR’s Ivan L. Nagy back in February, the guys in this world are “symptomatic of the nihilistic stream of slop that is going viral now.” Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death , a fascinating new docuseries released by Hulu on Tuesday, explores the origins of looksmaxxing, tracing its roots to a controversial fitness personality named Anthony Hughes, better known online as Tony Huge. A biohacking guru with cartoonishly large muscles and a devoted online following, Huge lives in Thailand surrounded by a harem of women and alpha males who seek his counsel. His methods are an extreme expression of toxic masculinity, literally fueled by steroids, peptides, amphetamines, meth, ketamine, and other drugs. “Women have been dealing with these unhealthy, toxic beauty and health standards forever. And now it’s happening quickly with men, because you can’t go online without your insecurities being preyed on,” Jennings Brown , an executive producer on the series and the journalist who developed the show, told me. “These men are taking it to such a toxic, extreme level that they’re dying or having heart attacks in their twenties and thirties or other strange pulmonary-health issues, because they want to increase their SMV, their sexual market value.” Huge emerges as a modern-day Dr. Frankenstein, seemingly unable to understand the creatures he has spawned or to confront the destructive consequences of his experimental practices. In one particularly telling scene, he appears genuinely shocked by the extreme surgeries that Androgenic, the second most popular looksmaxxer, is planning to undergo while in Thailand. When some of the influencers in Huge’s orbit begin dying under mysterious circumstances, he seems incapable of processing their deaths or considering his own possible culpability. At times, the project can feel like a lurid dispatch from a world so detached from reality that it’s hard to see its relevance to the broader culture. But the influence of looksmaxxing on young men cannot be overstated. It has become enormously popular among adolescent boys in recent years, bringing with it very real risks to their physical and mental health. “Body dysmorphia is very popular now, and it’s kind of in everything. It’s affecting men in a way that it’s always affected women. We’re seeing it unfold in unusual ways that we aren’t really prepared for as a society,” Jennings told me. “It bleeds into everything.” If you have a suggestion for this column, please send it to laurelsanddarts@cjr.org . results.evidenceText: Longtime NBC Sports commentator Dan Hicks passes away at 64 Skip to content Credit: USA Today Network Pictures Archive By Drew Lerner on 11/12/2026 Less AI and more AA in your search results. The sports media world was sent into a state of shock on Thursday morning as longtime NBC Sports commentator Dan Hicks passed away at 64. Prior to his sudden passing, Hicks served as the lead play-by-play voice of NBC Sports’ PGA Tour coverage, returned as the lead voice of Notre Dame football in 2024, and was also the voice of several prominent Olympic sports for NBC including swimming and skiing. He spent over three decades at NBC after beginning his national TV career as a sports reporter at CNN. Hicks was married to veteran ESPN broadcaster Hannah Storm. Statements on Hicks’ devastating passing poured out on Thursday morning, beginning with his wife. https://t.co/8CK7OLXbZx — Hannah Storm (@HannahStormESPN) November 12, 2026 “Our family is heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected passing of Dan following an acute illness. He was a devoted husband over 30 years, loving father to our three daughters, and cherished friend to so many. His loss is immeasurable,” Storm said in a statement. “Dan was truly one of a kind and, quite simply, the person everyone wanted to be around. When he walked into a room, he brought the energy, the laughter and the people together. He was endlessly kind, thoughtful and funny, and he made everyone feel like they mattered. Our three daughters and I are heartbroken. We are grateful for the love and support surrounding our family during this incredibly difficult time. There are simply no words to express how much he will be missed.” Rich Lerner, Hicks’ longtime colleague at NBC Sports and Golf Channel, announced the news on Golf Channel on Thursday morning. Rich Lerner announces on Golf Channel that longtime NBC Sports broadcaster Dan Hicks has passed away at 64. Hicks was the longtime lead play-by-play voice of the PGA Tour, Notre Dame football, and Olympic swimming and skiing on NBC. https://t.co/45HBapuMhg — Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) November 12, 2026 Hicks called any number of legendary moments throughout his career. Among them was his memorable call on the 72nd hole of the 2008 U.S. Open, when Tiger Woods rolled in a 12-foot birdie putt to tie Rocco Mediate and force a playoff the next day. “Expect anything different!?” Hicks bellowed in a call that would live on forever. The “EXPECT ANYTHING DIFFERENT?” call from Dan Hicks after the Tiger birdie on the 72nd hole at 2008 US Open at Torrey to force a playoff with Rocco Mediate never gets old🔥 As the US Open resumes at Oakmont, appreciate the greatness of @DanHicksNBC 🫡 https://t.co/6zEdHNZAdl — Jack Benjamin (@JackBenjaminPxP) June 15, 2025 Hicks was also the voice of Michael Phelps’ legendary Olympic run in 2008 when the swimmer won a record-setting eight gold medals. On the winter side of things, Hicks voiced Lindsey Vonn’s dominant run in alpine skiing. NBC Sports president Rick Cordella, and executive producers Sam Flood and Molly Solomon also released a statement on Thursday. https://t.co/nEscSk889a — NBC Sports PR (@NBCSportsPR) November 12, 2026 The PGA Tour also released a statement mourning Hicks. https://t.co/Uy2Gm3FFxi — PGA Tour (@PGATour) November 12, 2026 The outpouring of support among former colleagues has been heavy and swift. Golf Channel remains in breaking news coverage about Hicks’ passing at the time of this writing. RIP. results.evidenceText: Inside the Supply Chain Funneling Irish Alumina to Russian Rockets | OCCRP Inside the Supply Chain Funneling Irish Alumina to Russian Rockets Investigation Leaked transaction data reveals how a major refinery in Ireland feeds into the aluminum supply chain of Russian weapons manufacturers arming Putin’s forces as they attack Ukraine. Banner: James O’Brien/OCCRP Banner: James O’Brien/OCCRP Key Findings Europe’s largest refinery of alumina — the main raw material used to make aluminum — has been sending the majority of its exports to Russian smelters that feed into the supply chain of EU-sanctioned arms manufacturers. The Ireland-based plant, Aughinish Alumina, has increased its exports to Russian smelters since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Once in Russia, the alumina is processed into aluminum and sold to clients that include a Moscow-based trader which has supplied hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of aluminum to Russian arms manufacturers, leaked transaction data shows. These arms manufacturers include more than 40 firms that have been sanctioned by the EU, and whose weapons have killed thousands of civilians and caused widespread damage in Ukraine. Despite the EU’s calls for member states to stockpile alumina due to its importance in industry and defense, the bloc has not placed restrictions on the raw material's export to Russia. Reported by Eli Moskowitz OCCRP Misha Gagarin OCCRP Ingrid Gercama OCCRP Conor Gallagher The Irish Times iStories March 24, 2026 Along a rugged, wind-swept shore in western Ireland stands Aughinish Alumina, the hulking industrial complex that is Europe's largest alumina refinery. Inside the sprawling plant, heat and pressure are harnessed to transform bauxite — a reddish rock mined oceans away — into alumina, the main raw material needed to produce aluminum. Strong and resistant to corrosion, aluminum is vital for manufacturing military hardware like missiles, drones, and aircraft. That’s one reason why the European Commission has called on member states to stockpile alumina as a defense against hostile powers. Yet rather than remaining in the European Union, the majority of the Aughinish factory’s exports are shipped to Russia’s largest aluminum smelters. Those smelters, in turn, feed into a supply chain of sanctioned defense contractors whose weapons have killed thousands of civilians in Ukraine, a new investigation by OCCRP and partners has found. Credit: Alan Betson/The Irish Times View of the Aughinish Alumina refinery in County Limerick, Ireland. Reporters could not track the final destination of a specific batch of Aughinish’s alumina, as the powdery substance is typically mixed together with alumina from other sources in the smelting process. However, customs and trade data show that since 2023, more than half the Ireland-based refinery’s alumina exports have gone to smelters in Russia owned by the plant’s Russian parent company, United Company Rusal. After processing the alumina into aluminum, the smelters have sold more than $650 million worth of the metal to a Moscow-based trader, Aluminium Sales Company (ASK), which supplies aluminum to clients that include dozens of EU-sanctioned Russian weapons manufacturers, according to leaked transaction data. (The data does not detail the volume of aluminum sold.) Weapons made by these firms have leveled entire city blocks in Mariupol, struck a children’s hospital in Kyiv, and blown open an apartment building in western Ukraine, according to EU sanctions listings, Ukraine’s military intelligence, and the London-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI). Aughinish Alumina's exports to Russia — which have increased since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — are entirely legal under EU trade rules. That is because despite the bloc’s recognition of alumina’s importance, no restrictions have been placed on the product’s export to Russia. The EU banned imports of aluminum produced in Russia in February 2025 in an effort to sever an income stream that could be used to fund Moscow’s war. But it has not prohibited the export of alumina to Russia, despite calls from the Latvian government which argued that a ban would “weaken [Russia’s] war machine.” When reached for comment, Aughinish told OCCRP that it operates “in strict compliance with all applicable European Union laws, including sanctions, export control measures and trade regulations.” The company said it had implemented “robust sanctions compliance and due diligence framework covering its entire supply chain,” though it did not respond to specific questions about whether its products might be used to build Russian weapons. The firm emphasized that alumina and aluminum are basic commodities serving “broad general purpose societal needs…vital for countless civilian industries.” Alex Prezanti, a U.K. barrister and sanctions specialist, said the lack of restrictions on the alumina trade reflects the tightrope the EU must walk as it tries to stem the flow of money and materials to Russia without compromising the bloc’s own economic interests. “EU policymakers have to draw a balance between potential impact of sanctions on Russia and potential impact of sanctions on their domestic economies,” said Prezanti, a co-founder of the State Capture Accountability Project non-profit. No further action was taken on alumina “either because the EU didn't think that it would have sufficient impact, or because one or more member states decided that this ban was not in their national interests.” The European Commission did not respond to requests to comment. Credit: Narciso Contreras/Anadolu/Anadolu via AFP Medical staff search through the rubble of a destroyed building for salvageable items after a Russian missile strike on the Okhmatdyt children’s hospital in Kyiv, Ukraine, July 10, 2024. Credit: Narciso Contreras/Anadolu/Anadolu via AFP Medical staff search through the rubble of a destroyed building for salvageable items after a Russian missile strike on the Okhmatdyt children’s hospital in Kyiv, Ukraine, July 10, 2024. Ireland’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade stressed that alumina is “not a sanctioned good” and “therefore its export to other countries, including Russia, is not restricted.” A lack of data makes it “difficult to ascertain where Russia is sourcing its tools and weapons from,” a spokesperson said, adding that “Ireland remains unequivocal in its continuing support for Ukraine in light of Russia’s unjustified invasion.” Yet Oleksandr V. Danylyuk, a former Ukraine defense official who is now a fellow at the think-tank RUSI, sees a concerning contradiction. In his view, supplying Russia with EU-made alumina “could undermine NATO’s stated goals of supporting Ukraine and deterring Russia.” Pavlo Shkurenko, a Sanctions Research Fellow at Kyiv School of Economics Institute, also warns that Europe’s “entanglement” with Russia’s metallurgical sector carries serious risks for the continent. It enables "not only direct daily attacks on Ukrainian civilians, but also potential confrontation with Europe itself, as the development of Russian military industry suggests." Credit: Mykola Miakshykov/NurPhoto/NurPhoto via AFP View of burnt-out buses at a transport company depot following a nighttime Russian Iskander missile strike on Dnipro in central Ukraine in September 2022. Credit: Mykola Miakshykov/NurPhoto/NurPhoto via AFP View of burnt-out buses at a transport company depot following a nighttime Russian Iskander missile strike on Dnipro in central Ukraine in September 2022. The Russian Ministry of Defense, ASK, and Rusal and its parent company EN+ Group did not respond to OCCRP’s request for comment. How We Traced Russia’s Aluminum Supply Chain OCCRP and partners — iStories, KibOrg, De Tijd, the Irish Times, the Guardian, and Delfi — relied on public and private trade and vessel data to track how raw bauxite from Brazil and Guinea makes its way to the Aughinish refinery where it is turned into alumina, and exported to Russia-based smelters owned by the aluminum giant Rusal. Though reporters were unable to pinpoint the final destination of the alumina that passed through Aughinish, leaked transaction data obtained by iStories revealed how Rusal’s aluminum has been purchased in part by a metals trader — ASK — that sells aluminum to over 40 EU-sanctioned Russian weapons manufacturers to fulfill defense contracts. Show more ‘A Strategic Asset’ Aughinish Alumina’s Russian parent company, Rusal, is one of the world’s largest aluminum producers, with mines, refineries, and smelters across the globe. In Russia, it is the primary supplier of aluminum for the defense, transport, construction and electrical industries. After Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the EU sanctioned Rusal’s founder and former top shareholder Oleg Deripaska, a billionaire and close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, for his alleged involvement in companies working with the Russian defense sector. (Deripaska did not respond to OCCRP’s request for comment, but has mounted failed legal challenges to U.S. , EU , and Australian sanctions against him.) Credit: President of Russia Oleg Deripaska (right) and President of Russia Vladimir Putin in 2006. Credit: President of Russia Oleg Deripaska (right) and President of Russia Vladimir Putin in 2006. Rusal, however, remained untouched, sparking a debate in the Irish parliament about the company’s plant in County Limerick, which produces around a third of the EU’s alumina. “We appear to be protecting the Aughinish Alumina plant from sanctions,” then-MP Thomas Pringle said in April 2022. “That is hypocritical of us. If we need to protect that plant, the Government should be considering taking it over straight away and…take it out of the hands of the oligarchs.” The country’s then minister of state, Patrick O’Donovan, responded by saying that the plant “is not connected…to any sort of Russian empire,” and that it was a major employer and supplier of alumina to European industries. Rusal itself had actually been briefly sanctioned back in 2018 by the U.S. for its connection to Deripaska. The move sent shockwaves through the global aluminum industry and led to a surge in aluminum prices. Not long after, the U.S. agreed to delist the company after Deripaska reduced his shares in Rusal’s parent company to a minority stake. Ireland’s former ambassador to the U.S., Daniel Mulhall, told The Irish Times that he lobbied to keep the Aughinish Alumina plant open, as it was “one of the few European strategic assets that we had in Ireland” at the time. But questions over the refinery were raised again in 2023, when Irish lawmaker Réada Cronin asked why Russia was buying so much alumina from the country, given that "such exports are capable of assisting Russia in its invasion of Ukraine." Ireland’s then-trade minister Simon Coveney responded only by saying that the alumina exports were in compliance with EU sanctions. From Guinea to Siberia To trace Russia’s aluminum supply chain, reporters started at the source. Trade data shows the bauxite refined by the Aughinish factory comes from the West African country Guinea, where Rusal owns three mines. It also comes from a Rusal-owned mine in the Brazilian Amazon whose largest shareholder is the mining and commodity trading giant Glencore. (When reached for comment Glencore, which owns a 10% stake in Rusal’s parent company, said it was “unable to comment on Aughinish’s commercial decisions.”) After arriving by bulk carrier to Irish shores, the bauxite is transformed with heat, pressure, and caustic soda into alumina at the Aughinish facility. Credit: Alan Betson/The Irish Times Since the 2022 invasion — after which one of Rusal’s Ukraine-based refineries was nationalized — Aughinish has become an increasingly important alumina supplier for the Russian conglomerate. Credit: Alan Betson/The Irish Times Trade data shows that starting in 2023, the Ireland-based plant has shipped the majority of its alumina exports to Rusal smelters in Russia. Credit: sikaraha - stock.adobe.com The bulk has gone to two smelters in particular: the Krasnoyarsk and Sayanogorsk facilities in Siberia. In 2024, for instance, Aughinish sent around half of all its refined alumina produced that year — worth around $400 million — to Krasnoyarsk and Sayanogorsk, accounting for nearly 40% of the alumina imported by the smelters. That year, the two smelters produced over a third of Rusal’s entire aluminum output, according to annual reports. But that’s where the public paper trail ends, with Rusal making no public mention of supplying Russian arms manufacturers. Leaked transaction data, however, allowed reporters to follow the aluminum’s path. From Russian Smelters to Ukraine’s Frontlines The leaked transaction data obtained by reporters shows ASK paid Rusal’s trading arm more than $640 million for aluminum from the company’s smelters between the start of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 to April 2025. Credit: James O’Brien/OCCRP Credit: James O’Brien/OCCRP (While the data does not show the exact volumes ASK sourced from each smelter, it shows the trader also paid service fees to specific smelters for loading and unloading aluminum, some 40 percent of which went to Krasnoyarsk and Sayanogorsk.) Throughout the same time period ASK, in turn, made approximately a third of its revenue — some $337 million — selling aluminum for the purpose of Russian defense contracts. Reporters were unable to trace alumina from Aughinish to a specific product. However, ASK’s 2024 customer list included more than 40 EU-sanctioned companies — many owned by the Russian defense conglomerate Rostec — which produce weapons including anti-aircraft missiles, rocket systems, and long-range bombers, according to sanctions listings. Eighteen of these companies have built arms directly used in deadly attacks in Ukraine, said Andriy Yusov, an official from the Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, which analyzes the debris of Russian weaponry found on Ukraine's battlefields. One of the trader’s biggest customers is Kamaz, a manufacturer of heavy-duty vehicles used by Russia’s armed forces in Ukraine, according to its EU sanctions listing. In 2024, Kamaz paid ASK $16 million for aluminum, the data shows. Credit: Kremlin Pool/Alamy Stock Photo Russian President Vladimir Putin gets behind the wheel of a Kamaz dump truck at the inauguration of the Crimean Bridge highway on May 15, 2018, in Taman, Kerch, Russia. Credit: Kremlin Pool/Alamy Stock Photo Russian President Vladimir Putin gets behind the wheel of a Kamaz dump truck at the inauguration of the Crimean Bridge highway on May 15, 2018, in Taman, Kerch, Russia. Another top ASK client is the U.S.- and EU-sanctioned Votkinsk Machine Building Plant, which bought $101,200 worth of aluminum from ASK in 2024. According to EU authorities and Ukraine's military intelligence agency, the Votkinsk plant manufactures a range of armaments, including long-range missiles and the short-range Iskander ballistic missile — a weapon that reportedly killed 31 civilians in an attack in the northeastern city of Sumy in April 2025. Kamaz, Votkinsk, and eleven other sanctioned arms manufacturers that buy aluminum from ASK did not respond to requests to comment. NATO and EU leaders have issued repeated warnings regarding the strategic threat posed by systems developed by Russia's arms manufacturers. “Putin’s war machine is speeding up – not slowing down,” NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said last summer in a speech that highlighted Russia’s growing weapons production. “Let’s not kid ourselves; we are all on the eastern flank now,” he warned. “The new generation of Russian missiles travel at many times the speed of sound.” Khadija Sharife, Alina Tsogoeva (OCCRP), Kaur Maran (Eesti Ekspress), Simon Goodley (The Guardian), Maksym Dudchenko (KibOrg), and Lars Bové (De Tijd) contributed reporting. What the Logan Circle Shooter Told Me In a series of interviews late last year, Matt Lambert obsessed about his condo’s problems — and the man he killed. Police blocked off multiple blocks in the Logan Circle neighborhood. (Lillian Bautista/The Washington Sun) By Michael Brice-Saddler November 12, 2026 04:14 p.m. Email LinkedIn Twitter Copy Link copied Matt Lambert, a former emergency room physician and health care technology executive, shot five people and then himself on Thursday in D.C., apparently motivated by a bitter, ongoing and all-consuming legal dispute with the Metropole Condominium Association and the building’s property manager. The back-and-forth had been dragging on for more than a year, draining his retirement savings and fueling a deepening desperation. Just under a year ago, I spoke to him about it. Lambert reached out to me in late 2025 when I was a reporter at The Washington Post, pitching a story about how his million-dollar Logan Circle penthouse had been rendered unlivable. I continued reporting the story into the new year, but the article was abandoned when I was laid off from the Post in early 2026. In a series of interviews in late November and December 2025 — including two visits inside his gutted penthouse at the Metropole on 15th Street Northwest — Lambert described how a dispute over severe water leaks and black mold had turned into “psychological warfare” between himself, building manager James Stuart, the management company EJF Real Estate Services and their insurance defense attorneys. Trending Trump Taps Russ Vought’s Deputy to Lead Top Government Watchdog Trump’s Handpicked RNC Chair Is Under Scrutiny Over Hair and Makeup Services Amtrak Halts Service Around D.C., Citing ‘Local Municipal Officials’ Marco Rubio Snubbed Jensen Huang’s Outreach Before the Scandal Emerged “It’s affected every part of my life — my sleep, dietary habits,” Lambert told me in December. “I pride myself on my resilience, and I’ve been kind of surprised at how much it has been affected.” On Thursday, D.C. police said, Lambert shot and killed Stuart at the VIDA Fitness Center located on the ground floor of the building in a targeted attack just before 8 a.m., then shot four more people in the vicinity and barricaded himself in his apartment before shooting and killing himself. Of the other four people who were shot, one was in critical condition, while three others had non-life-threatening injuries. While at no point in the reporting process did Lambert give any indication he would resort to violence, he did frequently use intense, combative language — and at one point, his frustration veered into what at the time felt like dark humor. During a December visit with a neighbor, Lambert criticized the condo association’s legal strategy by making an offhand reference to Luigi Mangione, the suspect in the 2024 shooting death of UnitedHealthcare’s CEO who is accused of inscribing “delay, deny, depose” on his ammunition . “What are they called? Delay, deny, defend … the Luigi three?” Lambert said. Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region. Lambert, who bought the $1.1 million top-floor unit in 2016, had recently put the penthouse on the market with plans to relocate to New York. But he said the conflict trapped him in D.C., beginning after a building facade rehabilitation that ran from April 2023 to August 2024. While the project was underway, he said, water began running down the interior of his windows and wetting his floors after rainstorms — with cracks, peeling paint and visible mold spreading across his walls once crews finished work on his corner in August 2024. When he hired independent testers in October 2024 to show Stuart and contractors evidence of widespread moisture and airborne mold, Lambert said, the meeting ended abruptly. According to Lambert, when his attorney asked Stuart whether he could smell the mold, Stuart replied that the apartment “smelled like cologne,” walked out and turned the matter over to the building’s lawyers. Because my reporting on the dispute was not completed at the time, I was never able to present Lambert’s allegations to Stuart or EJF Real Estate Services to get their perspective. The Washington Sun was unable to reach the management firm earlier Thursday. In November 2024, Lambert said, he paid $12,000 out of his own pocket to strip his apartment down to the metal studs and subflooring, uncovering floor-to-ceiling black mold. When the building’s engineers blamed the moisture on Lambert’s own appliances, he said he went six months without using his shower, heat or dryer — instead showering downstairs at VIDA Fitness, and heating his unit solely with his fireplace — to try to prove them wrong. In March 2025, Lambert sued the Metropole Condominium Association in D.C. Superior Court, accusing the association of negligence, breach of fiduciary duty and nuisance over what he alleged were botched renovations and rebuffed repair requests. The association denied responsibility but lost a bid to have the case thrown out last year, court records show. When leaks persisted after rainstorms, Lambert said, the building’s defense counsel pivoted to blaming humidity from VIDA Fitness’s industrial dryer vents, which ran behind his unit, and moved to pull the gym into the lawsuit, delaying the case by another 90 days. By December 2025, Lambert, who was 54 at the time, said he had spent nearly $200,000 on legal and engineering fees — borrowing against his retirement savings to fund the litigation — while living with only a couch and a desk inside his stripped-down apartment. Lambert said in an interview at the time that he was preparing to have his attorney pull every email exchanged between him and Stuart for court discovery, accusing Stuart of giving conflicting answers to residents and fabricating maintenance history. Inside the Metropole last year, Lambert said the standoff had made him “radioactive.” He repurposed a whiteboard he normally used for work into a timeline tracking the building management’s slights. Feeling stonewalled by Stuart and the condo board, he launched an anonymous social media troll account called “Of Mice and Mold” to target Stuart and EJF over unfinished building repairs. He placed flyers on streetlights and trash cans around Logan Circle and hosted open houses in his gutted unit to show neighbors his engineering reports. He compared the building’s gossip and factions to being trapped in petty drama. “High school never ends. Michael, we are stuck in high school,” Lambert told me. “And it would be humorous if it wasn’t significant investment at risk, and really spending a lot of money that I’ve saved my entire life that I wanted to spend for retirement — I’m spending it right now with no end in sight. I’ve become increasingly aggressive in my messaging, not only in the building, but also with that Twitter page.” A Thursday morning post on the X account said, “My manifesto is an engineering report,” and contained screenshots of documents describing how problems with the facade and balcony had caused extensive leaks in Lambert’s unit. Standing in his deconstructed living room in December, Lambert pointed to a copy of Sun Tzu’s “The Art of War” sitting in his unit. “I go through every emotion every day on this. … Do I keep fighting? Do I not fight? And ‘The Art of War’ talks about, you know, the battle’s won before it’s ever fought. It says if you’re going to commit, don’t half commit, fully commit.” Lambert said part of the reason he was willing to fight was that he was a single man with no children. “They’re trying to make me quit. They’re trying to make me go broke,” Lambert said of the legal fight. “If I come out of this and I don’t get a satisfactory outcome, I won’t have a bunch of money, but I can live with that better than rolling over. … They don’t have my permission to treat me this way.” Raised in Appalachia by a single mother who died of cancer during his first year of medical school at Marshall University, Lambert worked as an ER doctor for 20 years before pivoting to health care IT. He moved to D.C. around 2010, later serving as chief medical information officer for major hospital systems in Seattle and New York City and working remotely as a chief medical officer for a Los Angeles-based health data company. During one December visit inside Lambert’s gutted unit, a fellow resident who had also been waiting months for leak repairs complained that when he called the management company, “you never get a call back from James.” Lambert immediately chimed in that he knew Stuart’s daily routine at the VIDA Fitness downstairs. “If you want to see the building manager,” Lambert said, “he comes in the gym about 8 o’clock.” Author Michael Brice-Saddler is a reporter at The Washington Sun.
