results.pageTitle: A crisis mismanaged: Inside 57 days of tragedy and turmoil at Arizona State
results.pageDescription: After a season-opening workout left a teammate on life support, men's hockey players lost trust in school leaders.
results.evidenceText: A crisis mismanaged: Inside 57 days of tragedy and turmoil at Arizona State - The Athletic Eamonn Dalton / The Athletic; Photos: USA TODAY Network; Zac BonDurant / Getty Images Investigation A crisis mismanaged: Inside 57 days of tragedy and turmoil at Arizona State By Katie Strang , Adam Kilgore and Nathan Fenno Nov. 12, 2026 Updated Share article 238 On Aug. 20, sophomore Matthew Mayich, a 21-year-old from Stoney Creek, Ontario, collapsed at the conclusion of the Arizona State men’s hockey team’s first workout of the preseason. He suffered exertional heat stroke, his family’s lawyer said, and remains on life support with no chance of recovery. Arizona State cut ties with head coach Greg Powers nearly two months later. The days in between represented a crisis of leadership at the university, The Athletic found. Arizona State chose to investigate itself despite calls for external reviews and allowed Powers and his loyalists to remain in charge of the team. With players left to find their own paths, the locker room splintered, with some fearing retaliation if they didn’t support the coaching staff and others concerned they were betraying a fallen teammate if they did. Advertisement This account of how ASU leaders handled the aftermath of Mayich’s hospitalization is based on public documents and interviews with more than 20 people, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared repercussions on their futures, both at the school and in the sport. Arizona State president Michael Crow, athletic director Graham Rossini and senior vice president James Rund declined interview requests for this story; a university spokesman addressed some specific inquiries. In a statement, Powers’ attorney said, “As has been the case throughout this situation, Mr. Powers declines comment until the University has completed its review and the ongoing independent investigation is finalized.” Day 1 Tim Ziesel, the man Powers chose to run the first official workout of the preseason, stood before the ASU players. Powers had bemoaned publicly and privately that last season’s team was “soft.” Ziesel, a former Green Beret, was brought in for what Powers described as a team-building opportunity. No one submitted Ziesel’s workout plan for approval, but ASU had signed off on Ziesel meeting with the hockey team. Ziesel had suffered a traumatic brain injury in 2023, when a drunk driver collided with his motorcycle; in a victim-impact statement submitted in court, he and his wife explained how the incident had changed him. The 2024 statement said he “struggles to gather his thoughts and have organized, complex analysis” and “has emotional regulation difficulties” that cause him to get “angry at small things.” Advertisement Running the workout as coaches looked on, Ziesel told the players his 8-year-old son could perform the drills better. He told the players their generation “had lost what it meant to be masculine.” He repeatedly said he was “dangerous” and bragged about how quickly he could “enact violence.” Ziesel declined to comment through his attorney, who cited an ongoing criminal investigation. Players stumbled and vomited. Mayich struggled, then collapsed during the final activity. When the ambulance carrying Mayich left Sun Angel Stadium, Powers told players they were “closer to making the Frozen Four” because of the workout and Mayich having pushed himself “to the maximum.” Day 2 Two more days of workouts led by Ziesel were canceled, but the team practiced — a 4-on-4 scrimmage with coaches watching from the benches. Mayich was on life support, but Powers told the players he had received “good news”: Mayich’s heart and other organs were in good condition, leading players to believe he would be fine. That night, a group of players went out to a bar, eager to decompress after an emotional week, awash in relief after Powers’ update about Mayich’s health. Players were still talking about Ziesel’s antics, jokingly repeating the line he used during the workout: “I’m dangerous.” Day 3 The school had not acknowledged Mayich’s condition publicly. On its Instagram account, ASU’s hockey program boasted that five Sun Devils had signed NHL contracts since 2025. Advertisement An ASU spokesman later said the school has been following federal privacy laws and respected Mayich’s family’s privacy throughout this time. Meanwhile, Crow emailed the Arizona Board of Regents with the subject line, “Student Athlete Health Alert.” He told the regents who oversee ASU that a hockey player had a medical emergency at 8:30 a.m. two days prior. “He has not recovered and is under intense ICU care. Reviews of the circumstances are underway. I will let you know how things progress.” That night, players gathered at an apartment complex for a meeting called by one of the team’s veterans, who delivered the news that Mayich no longer had brain activity and was not expected to recover. Some players started crying. Powers attended the meeting. He embraced players, kissed some on their foreheads and told them there was no playbook for what the team was experiencing. Among the last things he said: “I don’t want you to worry about me.” After the meeting, Powers texted some players individually to say how much he cared about them. Day 6 In media reports, Mayich was identified publicly for the first time as the player who collapsed. Matthew Mayich was selected by the St. Louis Blues with the 170th overall pick in the 2023 NHL draft. (Bruce Bennett / Getty Images) Day 9 Rossini, a baseball team manager while an ASU student and whose only college administrative experience has been at the school, visited the Arizona Sports 98.7 FM studio for an interview with the “Burns & Gambo” show. In the first public remarks he or any ASU leader would make about the situation involving Mayich, he made a clear distinction about how the university planned to look into the incident: “This is not an investigation. We’re collecting information. If there’s things we need to identify and learn from, we’re going to do that. But this is not an investigation where somebody is suggesting something went wrong.” Advertisement Arizona State tabbed Rund to lead the “review.” Rund previously oversaw ASU’s club sports, hockey among them. When a donor pledged the money to take ASU to Division I in 2014, Powers’ first call was to Rund, who secured a meeting with ASU athletic department officials. An ASU spokesman later said there is no conflict of interest between Rund giving ongoing advice and assistance to Rossini and leading the review. Ziesel’s representative, Buddy Rake, gave an interview to an NBC affiliate in Phoenix. Rake said: “There isn’t a D1 athlete on the planet that would describe this as a hard day of exercising, including the ASU hockey team.” His comments echoed the narrative Powers’ supporters were floating to media members and others in the hockey community: That the workout hadn’t been that difficult, and that players had ample access to water and rest. Day 12 Rob Carey, an attorney for the Mayich family, told The Athletic that ASU “seems to be circling the wagons” at the expense of uncovering what had happened. He requested Powers and his staff be placed on leave. “It’s very clear to me that this is a time when adults have to do the right thing — sometimes the right thing is the hard thing,” Carey said. “And from everything I can tell and the leads we have, ASU is not handling this responsibly.” Carey sent document preservation letters to ASU and Powers, instructing them not to destroy or delete any evidence relating to the Aug. 20 workout. In the locker room, players were divided, with some agreeing with Carey’s position that Powers and his staff needed to be put on leave and others defending the coach. Day 14 The Athletic reported that the ASU Police Department had opened an investigation of the events surrounding the workout. The school characterized this as standard operating procedure for a serious injury incident and declined to answer questions about who initiated the probe or how it would differ from the Rund-led “review.” Advertisement Several players were concerned. If they participated in Rund’s review or talked to police and said something critical about the way the workout was run or the handling of the matter, would what they said get back to Powers, who maintained control of their athletic careers? Rossini met with the players for the first time since the workout. He spoke briefly, telling players he was there for them and had been since the event. Said one player: “He then left almost as quickly as he got there.” An ASU spokesman later said Rossini and members of ASU student services visited Mayich in the hospital, including a visit the night he collapsed and in subsequent days. Day 15 Teammates gathered to support Mayich and his family during a vigil at the hospital. No members of the coaching staff were present. Day 16 Carey wrote a letter to ASU asking the school to refer the ASUPD investigation to the Phoenix Police Department, the Arizona Attorney General’s office or the Arizona Department of Public Safety to ensure independence. Rossini emailed ASU hockey parents, addressing a group that had been feeling largely in the dark. “I’m committed to working together with you through this and learning not only what happened but working to make sure this never happens again,” he wrote. Graham Rossini has served as the athletic director at his alma mater since 2024. (Mark J. Rebilas / Imagn Images) Day 17 Arizona State’s hockey program publicly acknowledged Mayich by name for the first time with an X post on its hockey account. Replies were turned off. Advertisement Day 20 In its nightly media report to the Arizona Board of Regents, ASU noted that interest in the controversy was fading: “Hockey questions still trickling in every day, but at a slower pace.” Powers and his staff appeared to have support from Rossini as they continued to oversee practices. But as Rund and the ASU police department began to contact players, many were conflicted. Some felt increasing pressure — from peers, from members of the coaching staff — to say nothing was improper about the workout despite feeling differently. An ASU spokesman said recently that Powers and his staff remained in place to prepare players for their season, support players’ well-being and allow time to gather more information regarding Mayich’s collapse. Day 25 Crow, the university president, departed for London ahead of the opening of a satellite campus there and the Sun Devils’ football team playing in the Union Jack Classic at Wembley Stadium. He commemorated the moment with a social media photo of his luggage. Day 29 The Athletic published a story detailing the workout that contradicted Powers’ version. The story also described Powers’ treatment of players last season, which included calling them “soft” and “pussies” and disparaging them in text messages and in signs posted in the facility. Day 30 Like Crow, Rossini kept his plans to travel overseas with the football team. Seeking a way to get school leaders’ attention, some players discussed sharing concerns they had about the coaching staff directly with Crow. Advertisement Transfer forward Daniel Shlaine, whose brother previously played for Powers, was quoted in College Hockey News saying the workout “wasn’t physically exhausting, more mentally exhausting.” Another player echoed his support of Powers anonymously in the story. The divide within the team deepened. Day 34 Arizona State released the initial findings of Rund’s review. It cited policy violations that included a failure to submit Ziesel’s workout to the strength and conditioning staff for approval and not following the school’s heat-safety procedures. But the initial report held no one responsible and offered only one actionable promise: the creation of a “blue-ribbon advisory panel” to give “recommendations” for future outdoor activities and the use of outside consultants. The report repeatedly misspelled Ziesel’s name as “Zeisel.” Carey called the review “mind-boggling.” Some players began to discuss among themselves what they had told police or university officials about the workout. They noticed that some of those details — including the lack of water for some teammates, including Mayich — were not included in Rund’s report, which angered and frustrated them. Later that night, Arizona’s Family Sports television network published a video from the workout showing several players who appeared to be in distress and in direct sunlight. Mayich could be seen struggling, at one point crumpling into the grass. Advertisement Day 35 Powers spoke publicly for the first time since the workout. In a virtual news conference as part of the National College Hockey Conference’s media day, he refused to answer several questions about the workout and touted ASU as “still a great place” for prospective players. His session included an exchange with a reporter from The Athletic : “In talking to players that have played for you previously, they said that one of the things that has been a guiding principle and philosophy for you is accountability. How have you modeled accountability for your team over the past month?” “In a lot of ways,” Powers said. “Can you expand on that?” “No. Not today.” Day 36 Powers texted contacts in the hockey community to let them know he had a new phone number. He told ASU that he had been receiving death threats and harassing phone calls. Day 39 At least seven players met with attorney Tim Casey at a local hotel to share concerns about the coaching staff and sign attestations about what took place on Aug. 20. They also said they feared retribution from the coaching staff. Advertisement The letter, which portrayed the school’s “review” as a whitewash, prompted two state legislators, including Rep. Arizona Board of Regents chair Doug Goodyear forwarded Gress’ letter and the players’ report to regent Lee Stein, a high-profile Phoenix attorney. “I’d like to talk with you about this tomorrow,” Goodyear wrote to Stein. Day 41 Team members, still practicing daily under Powers and his staff, were on edge after the letter became public. A players-only meeting in the locker room grew contentious as some team members demanded to know who signed the letter to Crow, bemoaning the lack of trust it created. One player told the team he believed the Mayich family did not want any adverse action taken against Powers and his staff. In response, the family later released a statement: “(The) coaches who ran that workout on August 20 need to be removed while an independent investigation gets to the truth. The players shouldn’t have to worry about retaliation from the people they report to every day.” Day 42 Arizona State placed Powers on paid administrative leave . Rossini issued a statement that did not mention the letter to Crow. “After thorough and careful deliberation, I believe this is the best move to provide stability for the hockey program,” the statement said. Rossini named assistant Mike Corbett the temporary head coach. After that announcement, The Athletic reported that Corbett had been charged with driving under the influence twice, including a few months after starting at ASU in 2024. He pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor count of driving under the influence but kept his job. Asked by The Athletic when the school became aware of that DUI conviction or another that Corbett had in 2006, the school declined to answer. Alex Hicks — a longtime Powers confidant whom Carey referred to as Powers’ “proxy” — and Jimmy Mullin, Powers’ other assistant, also remained with the program. Day 43 Rossini went on Arizona Sports 98.7 FM to explain placing Powers on leave two days before the season opener. He said he had done so to limit “distractions” for players. Rossini told the station he would hire an interim coach to replace Powers, a key distinction. Players can enter the transfer portal midseason only if their program hires a new permanent head coach. If the school instead names an interim coach, they are not permitted to transfer until the offseason. Crow met in closed session with the Arizona Board of Regents as calls mounted for ASU to take action. Day 44 Ceding to mounting pressure, Arizona State retained former Arizona Supreme Court Chief Justice Scott Bales to review what happened to Mayich. Even that announcement sparked confusion. The school communicated the development by releasing a letter from Rund to Crow that described Bales’ duties as reviewing policies and procedures related to outdoor athletic activities and the use of outside consultants. It took six weeks, two U.S. senators, legislative committee chairs, and the Board of Regents to get there, and ASU has again failed to do what is necessary.” That night, the Sun Devils opened their season with a victory at Lindenwood. Hicks, the assistant coach and Powers’ confidant, glared at players and stared them down at practice. Multiple people made university officials, including Rossini, aware of Hicks’ behavior. Day 50 Hicks left the program. The school would not say whether he was placed on leave or quit. Hicks did not respond to multiple messages seeking comment. Day 51 The Sun Devils lost their home opener to Holy Cross, 2-1, with Corbett serving as ASU’s temporary coach. “People can say what they want to say about the coaching staff or me personally and dig up things and that’s their prerogative to do that,” Corbett said in the postgame news conference. “We hurt, too. We are human beings, too. We were there, too, and we hurt.” Day 56 Powers’ nearly two-decade run leading ASU’s hockey program came to an end. He signed a separation agreement that will pay him 75 percent of the reported five-year, $2.5 million deal he signed in 2022, as well as two bonuses totaling $85,000. Advertisement The agreement requires Powers to cooperate with the school in any legal matter, including providing records and appearing for depositions or trials. Day 57 Dave Hakstol was announced as the new head coach of the Sun Devils. Corbett was not retained, leaving Jimmy Mullin as Powers’ lone remaining assistant. Though Rossini had told players he’d hire an interim coach, Hakstol was named as ASU’s permanent coach. By then, most players had appeared in at least one game. results.evidenceText: Paraguayan President Impeached and Arrested Amid Financial Meltdown and Mass Protests | OCCRP Power and Influence • Paraguay Paraguayan President Impeached and Arrested Amid Financial Meltdown and Mass Protests Former Paraguayan President Santiago Peña has been removed from office and arrested. Among other allegations, he is accused of trying to protect a digital bank he formerly held ownership in. Authorities this week ordered it into insolvency, leaving millions of citizens without access to their accounts. Banner: Shufu Liu/Office of the President/Taiwan Presidential Office/Flickr | Former Paraguayan President Santiago Peña Reported by Aldo Benitez OCCRP November 7, 2026 | 2 min read Share Article × Aa Text Settings × Text Size Small Medium Large Line Spacing Compact Normal Spacious Paraguayan President Santiago Peña has been impeached and arrested amid a financial crisis that triggered mass protests, and turned his own Colorado party against him. The crisis was sparked by a major digital bank being ordered into insolvency earlier in the week. Peña previously had shares in the holding company that owned the digital lender, Ueno Bank. Peña has denied allegations that he helped protect Ueno from scrutiny. In addition to holding public funds, Ueno banked millions of private citizens who have now been left without access to their accounts. In a Thursday statement announcing his resignation, posted to Facebook, Peña said his “greatest wish” was that funds would be returned to Ueno customers. He said he was resigning in order to "bring calm to the population." By that time, the streets of downtown Asunción, the nation's capital, were teeming with protesters. In the Chamber of Deputies, both his allies and opponents rejected Peña’s resignation, and instead proceeded with an impeachment process. The matter then fell to senators who held an extraordinary session on Friday. Peña did not appear in person for his defense in the Senate, though he sent his lawyer, Ricardo Preda. Preda argued that Peña was “accused of actions that correspond to institutions, such as the Central Bank of Paraguay and the Social Security Institute, over which the president has no power or influence,” according to a report published by the Senate. The Senate rejected Peña's resignation, voting unanimously in favor of impeachment on the grounds of malfeasance in office, according to the report documenting the proceedings. Under the Paraguayan Constitution, the distinction between accepting a resignation and conducting an impeachment trial is fundamental. Had the Senate accepted his resignation, Peña would have retained his immunity, which would have shielded him from any judicial investigation. Following the impeachment, the National Police immediately issued an arrest warrant for Peña, who is charged with breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds. Peña was placed under house arrest, and police were posted around his home as a large group of protesters gathered outside. Peña will be succeeded by Pedro Alliana, who must complete the remainder of the presidential term that began in 2023 and runs until August 2028. Alliana will now have to address the economic crisis that has plunged the country into turmoil. "Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," Alliana reportedly said. results.pageTitle: Jensen Huang is out. The scandal is just beginning.
results.evidenceText: Jensen Huang is out. The scandal is just beginning. View in browser Top stories on Tech Policy Press Good morning! The biggest news in tech over the past week is the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and the various scandals that surround it. Even as details continue to emerge over Huang’s affairs and business deals, questions are swirling around the Trump administration’s handling of the situation, and over whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick acted to shield Nvidia. Despite his misdeeds, Huang still has his supporters in Silicon Valley—including Elon Musk and other men who don’t think his mistakes should have resulted in his resignation. President Donald Trump , perhaps unsurprisingly, had urged Huang to fight for his job. One question is how the controversy will affect US-China relations, specifically US policy toward China on chips and AI more generally. On Tech Policy Press, Georgetown’s Mark MacCarthy wrote about what Jensen Huang’s resignation means for next week’s US-China talks in Shenzen: tighter US export controls appear likely, but the AI safety dialogue still seems on track. “Huang’s downfall will also reignite the debate over banning Chinese open-weight models. Nvidia was one of the leading voices defending open-weight models, even when there was reportedly a push in Washington to ban them,” he writes. While Huang's resignation dominated global headlines, EU leaders gathered in Dublin on Friday for the bloc's first dedicated discussion on AI, seeking to strengthen Europe's AI sovereignty and reduce its dependence on foreign technology providers. Yet Ireland's approach raises questions about these ambitions. Layla Wade writes that Ireland, which holds the Council presidency, is drafting revisions to the Cloud and AI Development Act that could favor the Big Tech firms Europe wants to depend on less. Beyond questions of infrastructure and industrial policy, Europe's reliance on foreign technology providers also raises security concerns. Tech Policy Press fellow Liz Carolan explored how the Dublin summits brought these challenges into focus, from the disruption of Ukraine's access to Starlink to Europe's limited alternatives, highlighting the tension between competitiveness and safety in Europe's approach to tech policy. The European Commission also unveiled its long-awaited Digital Fairness Act (DFA) proposal this week, renewing debate about how to protect consumers from manipulative online practices. Four consumer law scholars, Anne-Lise Sibony, Fabrizio Esposito, Cristiana Santos and Cecilia Isola , assess what the proposal gets right and where its scope, coherence and capacity to protect consumers remain in question . Their analysis includes an original Tech Policy Press graphic mapping what the DFA would ban outright and what it would require companies to do. Itxaso Domínguez de Olazábal of EDRi writes that the proposal recognizes addictive design but relies on opt-outs, narrows protection for vulnerable consumers and does not clearly require companies to prove their practices are fair . ‘A New Agenda for Tech Regulation’ Multiple authors this week wrote about the opportunity to reform technology, particularly following the US midterm elections. Alice Marwick , director of research at Data & Society, asked leading scholars and policy experts what’s on their wishlist for tech regulation at the state and federal level — beyond AI. The answers span affordability, privacy, ad transparency, scams, data access and regulatory capacity. “Expanding regulatory capacity, passing comprehensive privacy legislation, and mandating data access for researchers may not be flashy, but these policies will have real-world implications for technology companies and, potentially, enormous benefits for the average American,” she writes. Greg LeRoy , who founded Good Jobs First, counts 44 of 45 local data center ballot measures passing by an average of 77% — and writes that incoming governors and state legislators have “a terrific opportunity in 2027 to enact effective reforms.” “Companies cannot both be a conduit when sued and a speaker when regulated,” write Allison Stanger , a distinguished endowed professor at Middlebury College, and Bruce Schneier , a fellow at the Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society at Harvard University, who propose three steps Congress could take on liability, amplification and disclosure. Richard Reisman , non-resident senior fellow at the Foundation for American Innovation, writes that “the platforms we call ‘social media’ are becoming increasingly less social” — even as AI takes over their role in filtering information. His proposal: treat both social media and AI as one project, and judge every piece of the whole by whose interests it serves. Will the AI-powered internet “remain open to anyone with a good idea,” or will visibility online “depend on the preferences of a few dominant platforms”? Jared Sine , chief strategy & legal officer at GoDaddy, on why open standards matter now. The US House Judiciary Committee under Rep. Jim Jordan has spent four years investigating disinformation researchers and Europe’s Digital Services Act. Tech Policy Press deputy editor Ramsha Jahangir and contributing editor Dean Jackson ask what changes now that Jordan is leaving the chairmanship. Big settlements, little accountability for Meta and TikTok States will receive at least $1.2 billion a year from Meta for ten years, and up to $16.7 billion in total. Erie Meyer and Stephanie T. Nguyen , senior fellows at the Center for Law and the Economy, say the money should buy the capacity to check whether the company is actually complying. Recent Meta and TikTok settlements may “define the invisible, state-backed rules shaping information access for a generation of young people,” Daphne Keller , director of platform regulation at Stanford Law School's Program in Law, Science & Technology, writes — struck in backroom deals with “no opportunity for meaningful public oversight or challenge by affected internet users.” (This is a substantial piece of work; I urge anyone thinking about the settlements to take a look.) On Nov. 12, the case brought by Abrham Meareg, Fisseha Tekle and the Katiba Institute against Meta returned to Kenya’s High Court. Wairimu Gathimba , a writer and researcher in Kenya’s social justice movement, on what’s at stake over hate speech in Ethiopia . The United Nations and AI governance Machines are already killing on their own . Next week, leaders gather at the UN in Geneva to decide whether to negotiate a treaty on autonomous weapons. León Castellanos-Jankiewicz of the University of Amsterdam: “If diplomats fail to negotiate a new treaty, ever more lives will hang by a line of code.” António Guterres is stepping down after a decade as UN Secretary-General . “His departure comes at a critical moment for global AI governance,” write the Center for AI and Digital Policy’s Merve Hickok , Marc Rotenberg , Ren Bin Lee Dixon , Idil I. Kaner and Tatjana Titareva . The selection of the next Secretary-General is crucial. Down the rabbit hole: the need for improved recommender-system controls The European Commission preliminarily found last week that TikTok failed to adequately assess and mitigate the “rabbit hole effect” of its For You feed. Cecilia Isola , research fellow at SERICS, writes about what the Commission’s findings mean for how recommender systems are tested under the DSA. “Ensuring that systemic risk assessments do not become exercises in documenting compliance requires scrutiny not only of the procedures followed, but also of the evidentiary basis and methodological reasoning supporting the conclusions reached,” she writes. Christoph Trattner , professor of information science at the University of Bergen, argues recommender-system controls should honor what users say they want now, and proposes three requirements: instructions that last as long as promised, targeted ways to suspend an inferred interest, and explanations of what fills the feed afterward. The OpenAI copyright fight 56 amicus briefs were filed in the OpenAI copyright litigation . A closer look at the briefs reveals the arguments at play in the fight over AI and copyright, who is making them, and what is at stake. Check out the graphic on the precedents referenced and let me know what you think. Anthropic kicks off IPO push Keith Porcaro , Assistant Clinical Professor of Law at Duke Law School, examines Anthropic’s dual-class structure : two shares with no economic rights control the company. He asks what the government would have to pay to seize them. “This vulnerability is not unique to Anthropic. Other AI companies with imbalanced governance structures may be seizable for less than their full economic value. This is the cost of concentrating control in a small number of people, while working on a capable, potentially dangerous technology,” he writes. On funding Black women public interest tech leaders Marking the victories of numerous Black women elected leaders, Fallon S. Wilson of #BlackTechFutures Research Institute writes a personal missive calling for “delusional funding” of Black women public interest tech leaders. More important news from around the world Cambodia’s government says no online scam compounds remain in the country. Tech Policy Press fellow Lam Le reports on how scam operators are relocating across borders, recruiting experienced workers through Telegram and rebuilding smaller operations. “The lack of protection for survivors of trafficking into scam operations has contributed to a humanitarian crisis, pushing some to return to scamming simply to earn enough money to survive. Meanwhile, the spread of smaller scam operations around the world makes them harder for authorities to detect and dismantle,” she reports. Yasodara Cordova , an independent consultant and part-time researcher at CTS-FGV, argues Brazil’s AI strategy is tilted toward supercomputers and centralized data, and that edge AI — inference on local hardware — deserves a much louder debate. “Brazil already has centrally standardized Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) that allows dozens of private and public companies to plug into shared protocols, such as the Pix payment system. However, another big potential for the country resides at the margins, in the opportunity to automate what already exists or create new manufacturing lines supported by edge AI,” she writes. Must reads ideas upstream of the AI policy debate Matthew Kirschenbaum , Commonwealth Professor of Artificial Intelligence and English at the University of Virginia, traces a line from 1970s phone phreaking to today’s agentic AI: in both, the vulnerability is the porous boundary between language and code . Eryk Salvaggio , a Gates Scholar researching AI and the humanities at the University of Cambridge, reads the “Pain Axis” paper behind the “AI torture chamber” fight . What it showed was “narrower”: a vector that encourages models to associate descriptions of pain with moral failure and worthlessness. Politics, government and social media influencers New York City can set the standard for how governments work with influencers, or it can keep improvising. Columbia’s Anya Schiffrin , author of a recent report on the subject, spoke to me about which way the city should go on the podcast. What we’re watching On Friday, Nov. 6, I moderated a discussion between Meg Young, PhD , Khari Johnson , Sareeta Amrute and Hannah Sassaman on how AI civics can help us meet the moment and realize a more democratic vision of public interest technology. If you weren't able to join for the event, the resources and recording are now available on Data & Society’s website. Are you a university student, PhD candidate, or recent graduate with an interest in competition law, economics or policy? Are you concerned about the dangers of concentrated economic power? Do you have views on how it could, or should, be countered? If so, consider entering the inaugural New Competition School Award for Best Commentary by November 30. The winning entry and up to three runners-up will be edited and published in Tech Policy Press. I wish you the best for the week ahead! -Justin Donate to Tech Policy Press Tech Policy Press PO Box 90173, Austin TX 78709-0173 United States You received this email because you signed up on our website. The RLRH East Africa Operations Manager role based at the British Institute in Eastern Africa (BIEA) is a mid-career position responsible for ensuring effective and compliant operations in Nairobi and in the broader East African region. The postholder will coordinate office administration, HR, and finance and compliance processes, while also contributing to organisational culture and learning, office expansion, and donor reporting. The role combines managerial oversight of three junior office, admin and finance roles with hands-on operational delivery, requiring a proactive individual with significant experience in non-profit operations in Kenya and/or East Africa. Responsibilities Operational Management (20%) Serve as the focal point for East Africa operations, liaising with RLRH colleagues in Oxford and Africa, and British Institute in Eastern Africa (BIEA) counterparts on human resources, finance, logistics, legal and compliance. Oversee daily operations of the RLRH Nairobi office, including administrative systems, office resources, equipment, and facilities. Maintain and update office and operations manuals, safeguarding and finance policies, and employee handbooks relevant to the RLRH Nairobi office. Monitor local operational risks (legal, financial, and security) and staff safety issues in Nairobi/East Africa, escalating concerns to the Director of Operations and Strategy. Support implementation of organisational knowledge management practices and digital security protocols, ensuring local compliance and staff uptake. Support the management and coordination of operational activities at the current and future RLRH satellite hubs in Kakuma, Kampala and any other future African locations. Support fieldwork safety and security procedures, including local risk assessments, practical safety arrangements, incident reporting and escalation, in collaboration with programme teams and relevant security focal points. Human Resources (20%) Draft, process and follow up on staff and consultancy contracts with BIEA and Employer of Record partners (organisations that legally employ staff on RLRH’s behalf). Oversee records of all contracts in budget and financial planners and the RLRH HR system (BambooHR). Coordinate HR processes, including recruitment, onboarding, offboarding, leave tracking, and performance monitoring. Support the development, updating, and rollout of HR policies and the staff handbook (leave, code of conduct, safeguarding, anti-harassment, etc). Provide staff training and onboarding support on operational systems and tools. Act as a staff wellbeing focal point and mediator, ensuring staff have access to wellbeing and DEI resources (training to be provided). Track and support the acquisition of visa, permit, and other legal documentation necessary for staff to perform their work (eg. Class M permits, Convention Travel Documents) and, where necessary, conduct in-person follow-ups with relevant authorities. Support the implementation of accessible accountability and complaints mechanisms by ensuring staff know how to raise concerns, understand the available reporting channels, and can access relevant procedures. Finance and Compliance (20%) Line management of the RLRH East Africa Finance Officer, overseeing financial operations related to East Africa activities while ensuring high-quality deliverables and professional development. Liaise with BIEA finance focal point, BIEA Kenya Country Director, and RLRH Finance Officer to ensure timely approvals and processing of payments. Ensure RLRH East Africa financial processes are compliant with implementing partner and RLRH finance policies. Approve and manage payments, procurement approvals, reimbursement confirmations, petty cash reconciliations, and planned spending tracking for East Africa operations. Oversee reconciliation of transaction lists and provide oversight of payments and financial reporting. Support needs during annual financial audits and ensure compliance with legal and donor financial reporting requirements. Partnerships, Grants and Programmes (15%) Support disbursement and processing of research and fellowship grants alongside the Research and Professional Placements teams, liaising with BIEA HR and finance colleagues for award approvals and grant disbursement. Work with external organisational partners to establish and manage subcontracts, research partnerships, and collaboration agreements for paying out funds. Alongside BIEA legal & compliance manager, draft and manage MOUs with external organisational partners, including financial and logistical terms. Support programme teams in identifying and resolving operational challenges affecting the timely delivery of academic programmes, outreach events, research, placements, training and other activities across East Africa. Office Management (15%) Manage team of three direct reports (the Finance Officer, the Administrative Assistant, and the Office and Events Assistant), and any additional operations colleagues or trainees. This includes day-to-day oversight, quality of work, and professional development. Create a healthy and supportive work environment for all RLRH Nairobi office colleagues, ensuring accountability and a positive office culture. Oversee the effective day-to-day management of RLRH office spaces, ensuring they are safe, functional, accessible, and fit for purpose as the organisation grows. Plan physical space across the Nairobi, Kampala and Kakuma hubs, identifying space constraints, and working with partners and colleagues on practical solutions as needs change. Support the oversight of office events and logistics, and serve as the operational point of contact for visitors and delegations to the RLRH Nairobi office. Strategy and Development (10%) Incorporate Nairobi and East Africa learnings into global operational and strategic planning. Contribute to donor compliance, narrative reporting, and yearly narrative reflections on East Africa operations. Support development of new offices and operational structures, with a particular focus on documenting growth strategies for replication of new hubs on the continent. Undertake additional responsibilities aligned with the role’s purpose and organisational priorities, as directed by the RLRH Director of Operations and Strategy.
